shipped.outcome_quote: When we use the new test scores, we find that variance is substantial at the start of kindergarten and does not grow but actually shrinks over the next two to three years.

blind_target.authors: Downey, Douglas B., Paul T. von Hippel, and Beckett A. Broh.
blind_target.title: Are Schools the Great Equalizer? Cognitive Inequality during the Summer Months and the School Year.
blind_target.evidence_quote: In this article, we replicate a well-known study of growth in cognitive inequality: the article “Are Schools the Great Equalizer?” which has been cited nearly 800 times since it was published in 2004 by the American Sociological Review (Downey et al. 2004). We carry out the same analyses as in the original study, but we use betterscaled test scores that can more plausibly compare inequality at different ages. In addition, we update the Great Equalizer study with evidence from a younger cohort of children who started kindergarten 13 years after the original participants.
blind_target.outcome_quote: It scored reading and math with a non-interval scale, which made it appear that score gaps grew dramatically from kindergarten through first grade. This replication shows that the apparent gap growth in the Great Equalizer study was an artifact of scaling. When we measure reading and math ability with something closer to a vertical interval scale, gaps grow very little. While the contrast between school and summer still suggests that schools do something to equalize children, the amount of equalization now seems rather small compared to the inequality that exists at the start of kindergarten.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The article explicitly overturns substantial inequality growth while retaining the seasonal equalization finding, with additional seasonal patterns inconsistent across cohorts. This is partial support and partial correction. It includes reanalysis of the original cohort and a newer independent cohort; classification follows the new-sample component.

blind_target.authors: Yi P, Park JS, Melton DA.
blind_target.title: Betatrophin: a hormone that controls pancreatic β cell proliferation.
blind_target.evidence_quote: First, we established that immunodeficient NOD-Scid (NOD.CB17-Prkdc scid /J) mice respond to the insulin receptor inhibitor S961 in a fashion similar to that seen by Yi et al. ( 9 ) in C57BL/6J mice.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Messenger RNA levels of betatrophin were induced about fivefold as determined by quantitative RT-PCR ( Fig. 1 B ), similar to what was published previously for C57BL/6 mice ( 9 ). However, betatrophin mRNA levels were not increased in gonadal white adipose tissue after S961 treatment as had been reported by Yi et al. ( 9 ), possibly due to the different mouse strains used or fat depots analyzed ( Fig. 1 C ). It is worth noting that the increase in adipose tissue betatrophin mRNA reported previously was not statistically significant ( 9 ).
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Mouse pancreatic proliferation and liver expression agree with Yi et al.; the authors explicitly contrast the adipose-expression result with that original. Under the codebook a tested finding explicitly contrasted cannot be omitted. Human islet nonresponse is an extension to a species whose response the introduction says was previously unknown; it is not itself evidence of failure to replicate a previously established human finding.
